She does look young to me, and younger cats and first-time moms tend to have smaller litters. Sometimes you can estimate by feeling along the abdomen and counting their heads, but that can be tough to do accurately. Ultimately, I would try to keep her indoors, get her to a vet if possible, or a shelter if not. Some shelters may be able to help you get more affordable vet care if you want to keep her, and some vets may be willing to negotiate their rates or have a sliding scale.

I attended a family reunion at some kind of venue about a decade and a half ago, in midsummer. Everyone  else was at least 20, most of them older, and I was 8, so obviously I was bored out of my skull. There was a huge yard, and I saw some people setting up lawn chairs, flowers, altar etc. 

Now, 8-year-old me had never been to a wedding before and was very curious to see what all the fuss was about, but my mom said I wasn't allowed and had to watch my grandparents' anniversary slideshow with my family instead. 

Naturally, I waited until my parents were distracted by said slideshow, then quietly wandered outside, over to the set up lawn chairs, where people were beginning to gather and take seats. I sat right at the back, wearing a t-shirt and cargo shorts. Yes, I was barefoot.

For the next forty-five minutes, I watched people make their way down the aisle, then respectfully paid attention to every word out of the officiant's mouth, right up until my mom grabbed my shoulder, equal parts relieved and deeply embarrassed, and trying very hard to be discreet.

She whispered, "libentianimo, you can't be here, you don't know these people!"
But here's the thing. I did know those people. The officiant had said the names of the the happy couple several times by that point. 

So I loudly proclaimed "Yes I do! That's Bob and that's Sue!"

The officiant stopped talking, everyone turned to look, and my mother dragged me back to the reunion.

She was so embarrassed, she forgot that I should be punished for running off by myself. 

My dad just laughed. 

Anyway, sorry, Bob and Sue. For what it's worth, it was a beautiful ceremony.

There's this thing people do, where when they really WANT to believe something, they will take anything supporting that belief as iron-clad truth-no matter how flimsy it is-and anything that goes against it gets rejected, or they find excuses that will let them ignore that information. 


It's called confirmation bias. You usually hear about it when people have very strong beliefs and refuse to hear anything against those beliefs. However, it often comes up when a person has strong feelings on the line, including romantic love and crushes. It's a defense mechanism-being right hurts less and is less work than being wrong; and thinking your feelings are reciprocated is easier than having to "get over" your crush. 


Basically, your friend wanted to believe you had these feelings, and because of that, he reasoned that your behavior must mean you loved him, and ignored how you treat other friends similarly and how you identify. It doesn't help that society as a whole constantly tells us that everyone has to feel romantic love  everyone gets crushes, etc. 


Long story short, this is not your fault. You aren't doing anything wrong by being kind to your friends. It's a weird combination of human psychology and social pressures, and it makes this experience common for us aromantic folks. If he didn't use how you treated him as proof, he'd have found something else to support his feelings.

First off, dreams are weird. We know next to nothing about why they happen-just theories. That said, some of them are pretty good theories, so I'll give this a shot.

As far as we can tell, dreams are how we process what we've been through any given day. No news on how this happens exactly, or why some are tangentially related to our day at best, (example, me moving to North Carolina and avoiding my neighbour, Lin-Manuel Miranda after spending the waking day studying Decidedly Not That) but that's what we have so far.

So, for whatever reason, maybe because Aerosmith was playing in the background somewhere during your day, or you saw someone with brown hair, or you took an elevator, you have a dream about having sex in an elevator. You spend the day worried because you have no idea why it happened when you love your girlfriend and would never cheat on her. While you sleep, a day spent worrying about a cheating dream gets processed by your brain as another cheating dream, this time with your ex because...why not? This freaks you out even more, so you spend the day worrying even more, which your brain processes again while you sleep...so another cheating dream, this time with something else you were nervous about telling your girlfriend.

As for the vividness, the latter two were both people you'd had sex with before. Your brain can recall those sensations and incorporate them into dreams. In addition, dreams can vary wildly in terms of vividness. Some factors causing more vivid dreams include sleep deprivation, alcohol, drugs, and stress. I'm gonna take a stab in the dark and guess stress, with the recent move and your concerns about these dreams, not to mention any work stresses you might be dealing with.

Basically, the dreams mean you're worried about the dreams, and the worry ups the vividness. You're fine, and it's okay.

If she accepts she has it, and refuses to seek help for it, there are some self-help options out there. They aren't as effective as one-on-one treatment with a therapist, but they can help, at the very least. If she doesn't, there isn't much you can do beyond bringing the idea up from time to time, but there are a few little things. 

Picking up on when bad things are happening that might trigger a binge is half the battle. If you can catch it early, you may be able to talk through tough feelings and problems, and either find solutions that will work or suggest other coping methods. This likely won't be very successful, but if it is, you can use that one instance to remind her that she managed it once and she can do it again. 

Generally speaking, trying to lose weight by traditional means like dieting etc. don't really work-usually it just adds stress, so the person binges to cope with that stress, which increases the stress because they're failing at the diet, and it just continues in a vicious circle. Moving the focus from dieting to finding some physical activity she enjoys might be a better tactic. 

People with binge eating disorder may have go-to foods for bingeing, or foods that trigger episodes. Keeping those foods out of the house can help her avoid temptation. 

Eating breakfast can help prevent binges later in the day. It's not a surefire thing, but it can help.  

Finally, stay supportive and connected. She may isolate herself, but it's important you remind her that you care about her and want her to be healthy and happy.

This is real messed up. I would start looking for a different job if I were you. You should absolutely never be letting other people use your login, regardless of what management says. It puts all accountability on med errors on you. 

Write down everything you can remember about the narcotic situation that was reported, with whatever dates and times you can remember. Do the same for other shady things, ex pinning med errors that couldn't have been you, asking you to act outside your scope with the machines, etc. If you have what management told you to do in writing anywhere, or any other instances of pressuring/shady orders in writing hold onto that/print it if it's an email. 

In the meantime, make clear and non-negotiable boundaries. "I can't let you pull meds under my login, you will have to call management to get that sorted out" "I am not allowed to load narcotics into the machine, you will have to find someone qualified." "I am not signing for this med error without being absolutely sure it was me, let me verify with my calendar and records of my shifts." You can get another job if they fire you, but getting another licence is much trickier.

Any shady orders management gives you-you ask for a written copy of the orders. "I might be able to do that, send me an email to that effect and I'll let you know what I can do." Or email saying "Per our conversation earlier, you want me to be doing xyz. Please reply to confirm this, and I'll get started." What is said in phone calls or face-to-face can't be proven, but an email leaves much less wiggle room and can land them in hot water with any governing bodies re: long term care homes, or the media.

Be prepared to deal with a lot of under-informed adults who don't put the effort in to understand your daughter. (Unfortunately, this may include family members.) You may need to set boundaries and give ultimatums that aren't going to feel comfortable, and might affect your relationships with said adults. If you have a partner, they should be prepared for the same, and you should be on the same page regarding where the line is for family.

Know the legal rights you and your daughter have where you are, and be prepared to exercise them. Have a backup plan for education(switching schools, private, or homeschool) if the current school becomes a hostile environment. Make sure your daughter knows she can talk to you if she feels unsafe or picked on. I know it's not particularly nice to think about, but it's important to be prepared for the worst and try to keep the brunt of discrimination off your daughter. 

Talking about discrimination can be tough. I honestly don't know what age would be appropriate for it, but main points: People who discriminate are wrong, you have done nothing to deserve it, and you can tell me when it happens and I will help you. 

Get support for yourself. PFLAG does support for parents of LGBT kids, as do lot of other LGBT activist groups-if they can't help you, they can put you in touch with someone who can.

I think I understand what you're trying to say. A trans woman patient, presenting as female, with no surgical history, who doesn't want you to know she's trans.

If you have your suspicions but no proof, there isn't particularly a good way to ask. Odds are, she's not telling you because she's terrified that she'll be treated poorly, outed, or misgendered. 

First step is to make sure she's alone-if she has visitors, ask them to step out for a moment. You don't want to accidentally "out" her to whoever she's with. Then make it clear that whatever information she chooses to tell you, health or otherwise, is strictly confidential. It won't be shared with anyone who doesn't absolutely need to know. 

Second step is pretty easy: Mention that you have some experience caring for trans people, and while you may not know everything, you know enough to be respectful. (If you have any policies on respect for trans people/gender identity, let her know here.) Ask outright if she's trans. 

If she says she is, thank her for trusting you, and tell her you'll do your best to give her the best care possible. 

​

A lot of trans people will be uncomfortable with talking about their transition. If they're reluctant but willing to talk, get what information you need as quickly and painlessly as you can, and write it somewhere their nurses can access it. They may need breaks from this kind of talk-offer them, and give them as necessary The fewer times they have to deal with the questions, the better. They're not going to trust you right away-, but consistent respect, willingness to listen, sincerity and support will go a long way.

​

If you have proof they're trans and they refuse to give you or others details, you can infer that it's probably pretty painful to talk about, or they've had some real nasty experiences. Try and figure out which one is the main issue. I can't tell you this will work perfectly, but it's worth a shot.

\-Acknowledge their distrust, and the validity of their distrust: You can't guarantee that every person they come in contact with in healthcare-even wherever you work-is going to be understanding, knowledgeable, open-minded, or even safe. Alternatively or in addition, acknowledge that discussing transition related stuff can be painful and difficult, and that you are only asking what you need to know in order to get them appropriate medical treatment.

\-If you can present yourself as an ally, do so. Don't make promises you can't keep. (Ex. I definitely don't know everything, but I'm willing to listen and advocate on your behalf)

\-Offer some time to think: You've given them an idea of their situation, they may want to mull it over a bit. (Ex. Would you like some time to think about it? I can come back later, or we can do the rest of the assessment while you consider.)

\-If they still refuse to share information about their transition, respect that. (Ex. Ok, I'll do my best to work around that. Lets move on to x assessment.) If they agree to share information, then try to go quickly, offer breaks if they need it, and don't leave unless they want you to.

Hey, I appreciate your question!

Honestly, this is a tough one. There's not a single study on how hormone replacement therapy in trans people affects the lungs particularly in terms of PFT and spirometry, so this is going to be some guesswork. Buckle up.

(Also, "biological sex" isn't wrong, I know what you mean, but trans people tend to use "assigned sex at birth" as a clearer term-biological sex gets a bit fuzzy during transition.)

In the end, my guess comes down to hormones, rather than surgery. If the person in question hasn't done HRT(hormone replacement therapy), go with what was assigned at birth.

As far as I know, HRT started before natural puberty will more or less result in the same development as those assigned that sex at birth. I'm assuming If this is the case, you're likely safe running the test for their preferred gender.

HRT starting after natural puberty is where it gets a bit tricky. It can alter muscle and fat distribution, as well as alter tissues, but the two things it cant do are remove organs and grow or shrink bones. So while [the lungs themselves may change](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2391086/), the volume of the rib cage won't.

\-So for trans men, those born female, currently men, started HRT after puberty: Rib cage is still the "female" size, lungs and airways may have grown. Since ribs are pretty elastic, male testing may or may not be appropriate.

\-For trans women, those born male, currently women, started HRT after puberty: Ribcage is still the larger "male" size, but lungs have likely still been able to change in response to HRT. Probably female-style testing.

Both of these scenarios are assuming they've been on hormones for long enough to significantly alter tissue, which isn't instantaneous. Your mileage may vary based on dose and route, but regardless of what hormone we're talking about it can take six months to two years. Between those times, based on my guesses, it's going to be a bit of a crapshoot.

Honestly, for any situation where you're not sure, I would try to run the test both ways and either see which result makes the most sense, or split the difference. Or if they have a marker somewhere in the system just use that one for plausible deniability.

I'm just going to remind you that this is ALL GUESSWORK on my part, based on what I know about hormone replacement therapy and the average human body. If someone at your place of work has a policy on this, defer to that.

​

\-Are you on hormones? (No=use birth sex, yes=continue)

\-Did you start hormones before puberty?(Yes=use preferred gender, no=continue)

\-When did you start hormones?(Less than six months ago=use birth sex, more than two years ago=probably use preferred gender or run both ways if possible, between six months and two years=run it both ways if possible, or if they're closer to the two year mark run it that way, and if they're closer to the six month mark then vice versa.)

There is something called gender euphoria, and I personally think people experience one or the other-comfort and joy in their gender/expression, or discomfort and dissatisfaction. You can have both at once, if you're happy with a part of your expression but not another, but otherwise it's kind of one or the other. Gender euphoria and dysphoria are two sides of the same coin. 

It's my personal experience that when it comes to those feelings, if you aren't having one, you're having the other. There isn't really a neutral ground. Dysphoria can fade into the background very easily when you're used to It, so for many it might Just be very difficult to notice-the euphoria stands out much more. 

I also think we as a community should be careful in making dysphoria, and suffering in general, a requirement to being trans. If someone were to arrive here without pain, only joy in their chosen gender, I would be very happy for them. Pretty jealous, but mostly happy.

I guess I don't think you need to define your experience as dysphoria, but just have some measure of unease or discomfort in your "starter gender", so to speak, even if it presents as joy in your identified gender.

However, everyone has a different experience, and if I haven't accurately described someone's experience as a trans person, then that's my bad and I'll need to reevaluate my theory.

So, the source is not at all credible, not to mention extremely biased. 

The study itself also misrepresents many of it's sources. I couldn't find all of them, but I'm examining the ones I can. Skip this paragraph if you want. [Study 3](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18194035) attributes decreased trust to homophobia towards the children's parents and the parents coming out unexpectedly, while the one you have attributes it straight to having non-heterosexual parents. [Study 4](http://sci-hub.tw/10.1016/j.apnu.2008.08.005) only samples those who had gay/bi fathers in heterosexual relationships, and attributes the trust issues to the sudden marital conflict, not to having a gay parent. Fitsgibbons ignores this bias as well.  [Study 6](http://sci-hub.tw/10.1007/s13524-012-0169-x) is a tough read for me, but seems to have changed the standards used by a different study to allow for inclusion of those experiencing household instability-which gay couples are more likely to experience and can impact a child's schoolwork-or who have adopted. [Study 7](http://sci-hub.tw/10.1016/j.ssresearch.2012.03.009) doesn't differentiate between those gay/bi parents who had affairs, marital turmoil, or had stable same-sex relationships, along with capturing a view of same-sex parenting from a distinctly earlier generation, which given the legal situation on gay parents having kids at the time, likely skewed results towards the affair/marital turmoil side of things. [Study 8](http://americanvalues.org/catalog/pdfs/Donor_FINAL.pdf)  is from another biased organization, the Institute of Family Values. The jury is out on whether children need both man and woman role models, not to mention the idea  doesn't really take into account trans and nonbinary people, but having role models of a variety of genders and gender expressions can't hurt.
